passages.where: The first marriage, told as the climax of the creation story. A man leaves his father and mother and is joined to his wife, and they become one flesh. Marriage starts as a new loyalty, stronger than the old ones.

Through the prophet Malachi, God tells men of Judah who were abandoning their wives why he no longer accepts their offerings. The LORD himself was witness to their covenant. Faithfulness in marriage is something God watches over.
James asks where fights come from, and answers: from desires at war inside us. Most quarrels are about more than their subject. They come from wanting something and not getting it.

Often read at weddings, these lines were first written to a church torn by rivalry and pride. Love is described by what it does under strain: it is patient, not easily angered, and keeps no record of wrongs.
In a short word to households, Paul tells husbands to love their wives and not to be harsh with them. Harshness is named as the thing that betrays love in a home.

Peter tells husbands to live with their wives with understanding and honor, as fellow heirs of the gift of life, and warns that their prayers can be hindered if they do not. How a husband treats his wife reaches into his life with God.
Written to a whole church, but no place tests it more than a marriage. Bear with one another, forgive complaints, as the Lord forgave you.
A saying about how quarrels spread. Starting one is like letting water through a dam. Wisdom stops a fight early, before it floods everything.

The Teacher is praising companionship, not only marriage: two can stand where one falls. Some Christians read the third strand as God at the center of a marriage; the text itself speaks of strength in being bound together.
Near the end of the Bible's love poem. Love is as strong as death, and floods cannot drown it. It is the Bible's own hope for what married love can be.

misread.taken: These verses have been used to justify control, harshness or abuse in a marriage, and to tell a wife in danger that submitting means staying and saying nothing.
misread.says: The passage begins with “Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (Ephesians 5:21); in some of the earliest manuscripts verse 22 has no verb of its own and borrows it from that line. The word Paul uses for submit describes a free yielding, not forced subjection. The husband's duty is to love “just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), which is the opposite of ruling for his own sake. Christians differ on what headship means today. No faithful reading of this passage makes it a warrant for harm, or asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.

whole: A hard marriage can be loud or silent. Some couples fight about the same three things for twenty years. Some have stopped fighting because they have stopped hoping. Money, children, in-laws, sex, work and old wounds pile up until two people who once chose each other feel like rivals or roommates. Many Christians in a hard marriage also carry shame, because their marriage was supposed to show something better.

The Bible is not naive about marriage. Its first married couple blame each other within a page of the fall. Abraham and Sarah, Jacob and his wives, David and Michal: Scripture is full of strained homes. James puts his finger on the root: fights come from desires at war within, wanting and not getting. Marriage brings two sets of wants into one house, and sin turns each spouse toward their own. Yet the Bible also holds marriage high, as a covenant God witnesses and a picture of Christ's love for his people. The gap between the two is where most marriages live.

So the wisdom of Scripture is not a technique but a way of loving under strain. Answer gently, and stop a quarrel early. Look for the desire under the fight, in yourself first. Forgive, and ask forgiveness, specifically and often. Treat your spouse with honor, as a fellow heir of grace, not an opponent. Get help early: a pastor, a wise older couple, a counselor. Many marriages that come through a hard season grow stronger for it. And where there is abuse or danger, the first duty is safety. Scripture does not ask anyone to stay in harm's way.

differ.share: Christians agree that marriage is a covenant before God, that husbands and wives are equal in dignity as bearers of God's image and fellow heirs of grace, and that abuse is never God's will.

views.name: Distinct roles
views.body: Many Christians, often called complementarians, read Ephesians 5 and related passages as giving husbands a particular responsibility of servant leadership and wives a particular call to support it, within mutual love.

views.name: Mutual submission
views.body: Others, often called egalitarians, read Ephesians 5:21 as setting mutual submission over the whole passage, and hold that husbands and wives share leadership in the home without fixed roles.

views.name: Divorce and remarriage
views.body: Christians also differ on when divorce is permitted. Many accept adultery and abandonment (Matthew 19:9, 1 Corinthians 7:15); many also count abuse as breaking the covenant; some churches permit no remarriage while a spouse lives.

differ.after: All of them call husbands and wives to love, honor and faithfulness. The Honest Answer “What does the Bible say about divorce and remarriage?” sets out the views at more length.

sit: What do you want from your spouse that you are not getting, and have you ever said it plainly and kindly?

prayer.lead: A prayer from Psalm 19 to pray before a hard conversation.
